strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing genuine gaps: emphasis on explanation generation, hotspot perception, and non-English language coverage fills real needs in fact-checking research
Rigorous data construction with comprehensive annotation pipeline (LLM + manual filtering, claim rewriting, evidence retrieval, explanation annotation) and evidence library of 66,217 entries
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple method types (traditional, LLMs, RLMs) revealing genuine difficulty of the benchmark (SOTA models achieve only ~72-74% verification accuracy)
Novel metrics (ECS and HCPI) operationalize previously unmeasured aspects—explanation consistency and hotspot-aware evaluation—addressing real evaluation gaps
Practical ablations and efficiency analysis demonstrate value of proposed components (e.g., DEA achieving ~50% reduction in reasoning time and input length)
weaknesses: Chinese-only language severely limits impact, reproducibility, and adoption in the international NLP community; no discussion of transferability to other languages

Explanation generation quality is alarmingly low (BLEU-4 scores 0.21-0.30); critical disparity between RLM verification performance and explanation quality inadequately analyzed, suggesting unresolved fundamental challenges

FactISR method is incremental (1-2% accuracy improvements) and tightly coupled to specific RLM architectures with reward decoding; limited generalizability and lack of theoretical justification for design choices (Eq. 1 parameters appear ad-hoc)

Evidence retrieval is an underexamined bottleneck: R@5 of 78.97% and 5-10% performance jumps with gold evidence suggest artificially difficult evidence library; evidence construction via LLM-based paraphrasing may not reflect realistic fact-checking scenarios

HCPI metric combines multiple components with apparently arbitrary weights (α=0.05, β=0.2, κ=0.15, λ=0.6) without ablation or sensitivity analysis; no validation that metric correlates with real-world hotspot perception capability
Data augmentation transparency issues: inter-annotator agreement not reported, annotation costs/time not disclosed, LLM-based claim rewriting may introduce systematic biases
Limited analysis and insights: no domain-level performance breakdown, error analysis, qualitative failure cases, or investigation into what makes hotspot perception or multi-hop reasoning difficult

Dataset composition undermines stated focus: 85% single-evidence samples underexplore reasoning; only ~15% retain hotspot indicators, limiting the benchmark's ability to evaluate its primary stated goal

Technical concerns: no statistical significance testing, circular evaluation (ECS depends on GPT-4o), lack of inter-annotator agreement metrics, and gold evidence results highlight that evidence retrieval—not reasoning—is the primary bottleneck

strengths: Addresses clear gap: First fact-checking benchmark with natural language explanations in non-English (Chinese) scenarios, combining real-world trending data with professional fact-checking sources
Rigorous dataset construction: Multi-stage pipeline with LLM voting, manual filtering, and quality assurance via 3+ independent reviewers per sample from prestigious institutions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests 6 diverse LLMs (reasoning-enhanced and general-purpose) plus existing methods, with ablation studies validating FactISR components
Practical relevance: Trending platform data avoids Wikipedia artifacts; diverse domains (health, politics, economics) reflect real-world use cases
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with informative figures, concrete examples, and transparent construction methodology
weaknesses: FactISR lacks methodological novelty: Primarily sophisticated prompt engineering combining existing concepts (CoT, iterative reasoning); Equation 1 underexplains iteration behavior and token triggering; no comparison to recent prompting strategies; missing sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters (Δ₀=20, γ=0.1)

ECS metric insufficiently validated: Manually categorized 5-level scale without learned components; no inter-annotator agreement for ECS itself; assumes categories correlate with explanation quality without evidence; evaluation via GPT-4o introduces potential bias

Missing human evaluation despite core claims: Paper emphasizes explanations for interpretability/trustworthiness yet provides NO human evaluation of explanation quality; relies entirely on surface metrics (BLEU-4 known poor for generation); cannot confirm explanations support fact-checking

Experimental rigor gaps: No statistical significance testing; crude label extraction via fuzzy matching with unquantified error propagation; zero inter-annotator agreement statistics for dataset annotations; absent error analysis and failure case studies

Dataset limitations: 7,643 samples modest vs. comparable benchmarks (FEVEROUS 87K); multi-evidence set only 1,131 (14.8%) severely imbalanced; trending data requires significant manual rewriting creating artificial claims; no human-performance baseline; temporal leakage risk (2020-2024 data vs. LLM training cutoffs unaddressed)

Weak analysis and unjustified claims: Minimal explanation for why inference-scaled models underperform on explanation generation; no domain-level difficulty analysis; 'evidence triangulation' term misleading for 2-component process; no ablation on template structure or parameter sensitivity

Reproducibility concerns: Dataset release not explicitly committed to; code availability unmentioned; some hyperparameter choices unjustified; inconsistent notation (7,643 vs 7,614 samples; ESC vs ECS)
